newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan central bank cuts rupee in surprise move.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan central bank cuts rupee in surprise move.

text.p: The State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) slashed 3.79 percent off the rupee's dollar value on Tuesday in a surprise move that bankers said reflected balance of payments difficulties.
The SBP, abruptly breaking a pattern of gradual downward adjustments, cut its rate to 36.9700/37.1549 to the dollar from 35.6200/35.7981 fixed on August 29.
In kerb trading, the rupee immediately plunged 1.20 rupees to 40.50 to the dollar from Monday's close at 39.30.
"The devaluation is contrary to expectations, as most people were prepared for a gradual adjustment, not a one-step devaluation," analyst Zuna Mansoor at ING Barings said.
"We expect the rupee depreciation for the (calendar) year to touch nine or 10 percent, and a worsening of the current account deficit, given in-elastic imports," Mansoor said.

A foreign economist, who asked not to be named, said SBP governor Muhammad Yaqub had apparently tried to foil speculators by delaying any adjustment and then devaluing the currency to bring it back into line with the SBP's dollar-dominated basket.
SBP officials were not available for comment, but Yaqub was due to hold a news conference later on Tuesday.
The SBP move preceded talks between Pakistan and the International Monetary Fund on the sidelines of the annual IMF-World Bank meetings in Washington later this month.
Pakistan is trying to persuade the IMF to resume disbursements of a $600 million standby loan which have been delayed by uncertainty about the 1996/97 budget (July-June).

The IMF, which has voiced concern about Pakistan's balance of payments position, wants Islamabad to explain how it will cut its budget deficit to four percent of Gross Domestic Product this year. The target was set in the budget unveiled in June, but various interest groups have since won tax concessions.
Bankers said they expected the rupee, which has fallen 5.31 percent since July 1 and 7.95 percent since January 1, to erode another three percent against the dollar by the end of 1996.
"I see a further depreciation of three percent by December," Maqsood Ahmed, senior vice-president of the private Muslim Commercial Bank, told Reuters.
He said the rupee's weakness was unlikely to boost exports substantially, but could encourage remittances from Pakistanis working abroad and help Pakistan's foreign exchange reserves.
Foreign reserves, including gold and Special Drawing Rights, fell to $2.344 billion in August from $2.463 billion in July, compared to $2.821 billion in August 1995.
Pakistan's trade deficit widened to $270 million in July from $95 million in June while the gap for the whole of 1995/96 increased to $3.07 billion from $2.257 billion in 1994/95.
"There is no sign of the external account turning around yet," the foreign economist said.
An executive at a foreign bank in Karachi said the central bank move could prompt foreign fund managers to slow liquidation of their equity holdings in Pakistan, and deter capital flight.
"It is likely to stop overseas investors from selling their stocks and transferring foreign exchange abroad," he said.
He said selling by overseas investors had dragged down market capitalisation at the Karachi Stock Exchange to 326 billion rupees by the end of July from 371 billion in June.
"They will now buy the same stocks at lower levels due to the difference in conversion of the dollar," the banker said. "Some of the stocks are now very attractive for them."
Pakistan State Oil traded at 320 rupees ($8.63) per share on Tuesday, compared to 390 on July 1 when the central bank rate was 35.0400/35.2152 rupees to the dollar, he said.
